title: Gods Who Emigrated
subtitle: Deities travel with the people carrying them
description: Gods move along trade routes, with armies, with sailors, and in the holds of slave ships. Follow a set of them out of Mesopotamia, across the Mediterranean, into the Roman empire, and then across the Atlantic with people who had no say in the crossing.

stops.title: Queen of Heaven
stops.narration: Uruk’s goddess is love and war at once, and nobody here finds that a contradiction. Both are appetites that overrule you. She descends through seven gates to the underworld, surrendering a garment at each, and arrives with nothing. To come back, she has to leave somebody else in her place. Her name will change four times over the next two thousand years. The job description will not.

stops.title: The Storm God Goes West
stops.narration: At Ugarit on the Syrian coast, scribes press the storm god’s cycle into clay: Baal defeats the sea, builds a house with a window in it, dies, and returns. Ugarit is a working port. Its ships and its scribes carry these stories down the Levantine coast and out toward Cyprus and the Aegean, where people hear them and tell them again under other names.

stops.title: Arriving Through Cyprus
stops.narration: The Greeks call her the Cyprian and the Cytherean, named for islands she is said to have landed on, which is an odd way to speak of a home-grown goddess. Her oldest great sanctuary sits at Paphos on Cyprus, the crossroads between the Levant and the Aegean, and her love-and-war pairing follows the Near Eastern pattern closely. Whether she descends from Ishtar or was shaped by long contact with her is genuinely disputed. The contact is not.

stops.title: Temples From Aswan to the Rhine
stops.locationLabel: Egypt, and the whole Roman world
stops.narration: An Egyptian goddess becomes, for a few centuries, among the most widely worshipped deities in the Roman empire. There are shrines to Isis at Pompeii, in Rome, on the Rhine frontier, in London. Her rites offer something the state cults do not: a personal initiation and a hope about death. Emperors alternately suppress and fund her. She emigrates with no diaspora at all, carried by soldiers, sailors and merchants who liked what was on offer.

stops.title: The God Who Became an Author
stops.narration: Hermes begins as an Arcadian god of boundary stones, thieves and travellers. Greeks living in Egypt meet Thoth, inventor of writing and keeper of the record of the dead, and conclude the two are the same god. The merged figure acquires a title, Thrice-Greatest, and then an entire library of texts on alchemy, astrology and the soul written under his name. Renaissance Florence will read them as ancient Egyptian wisdom and rebuild its philosophy around them.

stops.title: Iron
stops.narration: Ògún is the orisha of iron, and so of blacksmiths, hunters, warriors, surgeons, and eventually anyone who works metal or drives a vehicle. He clears the path, with a machete, through actual bush. In the Yoruba towns of what is now Nigeria, an oath is sworn on a piece of iron. This is a god defined by a material rather than a place, which turns out to matter a great deal for where he can go.

stops.title: A King Who Became a God
stops.narration: Ṣàngó was, by tradition, a king of Oyo (a real office in a real empire) who hanged himself and was afterwards worshipped as the orisha of thunder and the double axe. Oyo is near its height, and it is also deep in the Atlantic trade, selling captives down to the coast. The gods of this city are about to be carried across an ocean by the people it sold.

stops.title: The Luggage Nobody Could Confiscate
stops.narration: Yemọja belongs to a river in Yorubaland. Carried across the Middle Passage by people who had no say in the crossing, she becomes a goddess of the sea, of the ocean they were taken over, and is worshipped today as Yemanjá in Brazil, Yemayá in Cuba, La Sirène in Haiti. Millions of people were shipped west having lost everything they owned. The gods went with them anyway.
